<header class="hero">
  <div class="hero-water" aria-hidden="true"></div>
  <div class="hero-inner">
    <p class="eyebrow">A Pacific climate data story</p>
    <h1>Living with a Changing Climate Across the Pacific</h1>
    <p class="hero-lede">Pacific emissions add up to a small part of the global total. The ocean around the islands is warming anyway. The consequences arrive through reefs, coastlines, harvests and storms.</p>
    <div class="hero-pair" aria-label="Opening comparison">
      <article>
        <strong>0.0454%</strong>
        <span>of global territorial CO₂ came from 17 Pacific island countries and territories with OWID coverage in 2023</span>
      </article>
      <article>
        <strong>540,400</strong>
        <span>people were affected by Cyclone Winston in Fiji in 2016 according to the event assessment</span>
      </article>
    </div>
    <p class="hero-caution">These two numbers do not prove that one caused the other. They show the difference in scale between contribution and exposure.</p>
  </div>
</header>

<nav class="chapter-nav" aria-label="Story chapters">
  <a href="#emissions">Contribution</a>
  <a href="#warming">Warming</a>

<main>
  <section id="emissions" class="chapter chapter-light">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">01</p>
      <h2>A small share can contain a wide range</h2>
      <p>The 17 Pacific places included in Our World in Data produced around 17.3 million tonnes of CO₂ in 2023. That sounds like a lot, but it was only 0.0454% of the world total. This does not mean emissions are low everywhere in the Pacific. In 2024, emissions ranged from 0.1 to 86.7 tonnes per person. Most places were near the lower end, while Palau and New Caledonia stood far above the rest.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="emissions-chart" class="viz-frame" role="img" aria-label="Separate comparisons of global carbon dioxide per person and Pacific greenhouse gas emissions per person"></div>
    <aside class="reading-note">
      <strong>Keep the measures apart</strong>
      <p>These two datasets measure slightly different things. Our World in Data counts CO₂ released within each place, while the Pacific dataset covers greenhouse gases more broadly. They tell related stories, but the numbers cannot be compared directly, so they are shown separately.</p>
    </aside>
  </section>

  <section id="warming" class="chapter chapter-dark">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">02</p>
      <h2>Every complete ocean record moved warmer</h2>
      <p>Across all 21 places with complete data, the sea surface was warmer on average from 2014 to 2023 than from 1993 to 2002. The increase ranged from 0.21°C in French Polynesia to 0.49°C in Nauru. The overall direction is clear, but warming did not unfold in the same way everywhere. The rows below show each place separately, so those differences do not disappear into a single Pacific average.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="sst-chart" class="viz-frame viz-frame-dark" role="img" aria-label="Twenty one comparisons of early and recent sea surface temperature anomalies"></div>
  </section>

  <section id="cyclones" class="chapter chapter-map">
    <div class="chapter-copy chapter-copy-map">
      <p class="chapter-number">03</p>
      <h2>The tracks were already here</h2>
      <p>IBTrACS records 508 storm tracks across the South Pacific from 1980 to 2023. The map shows where they travelled and which storms reached the highest recorded intensity.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="cyclone-scrolly" class="scrolly">
      <div class="scrolly-sticky">
        <svg id="cyclone-map" viewBox="0 0 1000 600" role="img" aria-label="South Pacific tropical cyclone tracks from 1980 through 2023"></svg>
        <div id="cyclone-legend" class="map-legend"></div>
      </div>
      <div class="scrolly-steps">
        <article class="step" data-view="all">
          <p class="step-label">All recorded tracks</p>
          <h3>Five hundred and eight paths cross the basin</h3>
          <p>The archive begins well before the period shown here. The 1980 start keeps the view inside the modern satellite era.</p>
        </article>
        <article class="step" data-view="intensity">
          <p class="step-label">Recorded intensity</p>
          <h3>One hundred and three tracks reached Category 3 or above</h3>
          <p>The categories use the IBTrACS USA Saffir Simpson field. Agency wind standards differ, so this is an orientation layer rather than a trend test.</p>
        </article>
        <article class="step" data-view="events">
          <p class="step-label">Four storms in focus</p>
          <h3>A closer look at Pam, Winston, Gita and Harold</h3>
          <p>These tracks link the regional map to the individual storm reports later in the story. They show where each storm travelled.</p>
</article>
        </article>
      </div>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section id="reefs" class="chapter chapter-dark">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">04</p>
      <h2>Heat becomes stress when it stays</h2>
      <p>Degree Heating Weeks track how much heat above the local bleaching threshold builds up over twelve weeks. At 4°C weeks, significant bleaching can occur. At 8°C weeks, severe bleaching and coral death become likely. The calendar shows the highest annual value at eight virtual stations across the Pacific. Observations from the reefs are still needed to confirm whether bleaching occurred.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="reef-chart" class="viz-frame viz-frame-dark" role="img" aria-label="Annual maximum Degree Heating Weeks at eight Pacific reef stations"></div>
    <aside class="reading-note reading-note-dark">
      <strong>A heat stress measure</strong>
      <p>DHW captures both how intense the heat was and how long it lasted. Lighter years can include brief warm period with little accumulated stress. In darker years, the heat persisted long enough to cross the published stress thresholds.</p>
    </aside>
  </section>

  <section id="rain" class="chapter chapter-light">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">05</p>
      <h2>Annual rainfall alone does not explain harvests</h2>
      <p>Across 450 annual comparisons from 15 places, rainfall and crop yield changes had a correlation of just 0.04. In simple terms, they barely moved together at this broad national scale. Rainfall can affect harvests through its timing, location and intensity. A single rainfall number for an entire country and year leaves out too much detail to explain crop yield changes on its own.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="rain-chart" class="viz-frame" role="img" aria-label="Scatter plot of rainfall anomaly and annual crop yield change"></div>
  </section>

  <section id="sea" class="chapter chapter-dark">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">06</p>
      <h2>The sea level record moves into higher bands</h2>
      <p>By 2023, every record was above the reference level. Higher bands become more common as the chart moves forward in time. By 2023, all 21 places sit at +0.1 or +0.2 metre, showing how widely sea levels have shifted across the Pacific. The 0.1 metre rounding hides smaller changes and makes transitions look abrupt. Shorelines also respond to waves, storms, sediment and land movement.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="sea-chart" class="viz-frame viz-frame-dark" role="img" aria-label="Sea level anomaly bands for Pacific countries from 1993 through 2023"></div>
  </section>

  <section id="impact" class="chapter chapter-impact">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">07</p>
      <h2>One storm can touch most of a country</h2>
      <p>Reports on individual cyclones and annual disaster tables are compiled differently, so their figures do not always line up. Vanuatu in 2015 shows the problem. The annual table records zero people affected. The Cyclone Pam assessment reports 65,000 displaced. The gap points to different definitions or incomplete reporting, so the zero should be treated with caution.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="event-cards" class="event-grid" aria-label="Four Pacific cyclone event comparisons"></div>
  </section>

  <section id="response" class="chapter chapter-light">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">08</p>
      <h2>Electricity systems are changing at different speeds</h2>
      <p>In 2023, renewables supplied 94.4% of recorded electricity in Tokelau and 52.1% in Fiji. They were the only two of 18 places where renewables passed the halfway mark. This chart covers electricity generation. Transport fuels and other energy uses are tracked separately. Where available, the details include the SDG measure for renewable energy across all final energy use.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="energy-chart" class="viz-frame" role="img" aria-label="Renewable share of electricity generation in 18 Pacific places"></div>
  </section>

  <section id="explore" class="chapter chapter-explore">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">Explore</p>
      <h2>Follow one place across the story</h2>
      <p>Choose a country or territory to connect its ocean, rain, sea level, disaster and power records. Missing observations stay missing. They are never drawn as zero.</p>
      <label class="select-label" for="place-select">Pacific place</label>
      <select id="place-select"></select>
    </div>
    <div id="profile-panel" class="profile-panel" aria-live="polite"></div>
  </section>

  <section class="closing">
    <p class="eyebrow">What the evidence can carry</p>
    <h2>The bigger picture across the Pacific.</h2>
    <p>The 17 places covered by the emissions data produced less than 0.05% of global territorial CO₂ in 2023. Every complete sea temperature record was warmer in the recent decade, and all 21 sea level records ended 2023 above their reference level. Coral heat records show pressure building on reefs. Disaster reports show how many lives a single cyclone can disrupt. They also raise the next questions. How much did warming increase a storm’s intensity? How much did changing rainfall contribute to a harvest loss? How quickly is sea level rise reshaping a particular coast? Answering these questions requires causal models, long records and detailed local data. The results can guide early warnings, coastal planning, farming decisions and climate funding</p>
  </section>
